title: Anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction)
summary: Severe allergic reaction: help them use their epinephrine auto-injector at once, position them, and be ready for a second dose.

steps.text: Look for signs of a severe allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips or tongue, trouble breathing, a throat that feels like it is closing.
Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.
steps.detail:
Anaphylaxis always needs medical care, even if the person improves after epinephrine.

If you are alone with no phone signal, give care first: help with the auto-injector, then go for or send for help.

steps.text: Do they have an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen or similar) or epinephrine nasal spray?
steps.detail: Check their pockets, bag or belt kit, and ask. The auto-injector should be their own prescribed one; where laws and your training allow, a stock auto-injector can be used.

ask.q: Is an epinephrine auto-injector or nasal spray available?

steps.text: Sit them in a comfortable position, or lie them down if they show signs of shock.
steps.detail:
A person who is awake but struggling to breathe should be allowed to sit up or take whatever position feels easiest. If they are pale, cold, clammy, faint or confused (signs of shock), lie them down.

If they are drowsy or vomiting, or you cannot watch them all the time, use the recovery position.

steps.text: Inject into the outer middle of the thigh. Press the auto-injector straight in (90 degrees) until it clicks, and hold it there for 3 seconds.
steps.detail:
The person should use their own auto-injector if they can; help them. If they cannot, and you are trained or the law allows, give it yourself.

Check it is their epinephrine. Take off the cap and safety release. Hold the leg firmly to stop it moving. Place the tip on the outer middle of the thigh at a right angle and push firmly until you hear a click. Hold it in place for 3 seconds after the click (devices differ: follow the instructions printed on the device if they say otherwise). Then remove it and rub the spot for about 10 seconds.

Nasal spray (such as neffy): put the tip in one nostril and press the plunger firmly to give the dose.

Note the time of the dose. Keep the used device to hand over to medical staff.

Auto-injectors have a viewing window. Red Cross guidance is that a cloudy or discoloured solution should be discarded; epinephrine breaks down quickly in heat.
steps.warn: Note the time of the dose.

steps.text: Watch closely. If signs are still there 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose and help has not arrived, a second dose may be given. Under 5 minutes: wait for the timer.
steps.detail:
AHA (2024 First Aid guidelines) estimates that between 7 and 18 percent of people with anaphylaxis need more than one dose. A second dose uses a new auto-injector or nasal spray, given the same way as the first.

The Red Cross lay guidance gives 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose, if symptoms continue and help has not arrived. The AHA and Red Cross 2024 guidelines say a repeat dose may be considered if there is no response and help is more than 5 to 10 minutes away.

If less than 5 minutes have passed, wait for the timer, then answer the question.

ask.q: 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose, are signs still present, with help not yet arrived?

steps.text: Give a second dose with a new auto-injector or nasal spray, the same way as the first. Note the time.
steps.detail: Same site (outer middle thigh, either leg), same technique: straight in until it clicks, hold for 3 seconds, rub the spot for 10 seconds.

steps.text: Keep them comfortable and stop them getting cold or overheated. Treat for shock if needed. Keep watching breathing and alertness.
steps.detail:
Reassure them. Stay with them.

If they show signs of shock, use the Shock protocol: lie them down; if they are at risk of choking on vomit or you cannot watch them all the time, use the recovery position.

Even if they feel better, they must still be seen by a medical professional. Give the used devices to medical staff.

ask.q: Have they become unresponsive and stopped breathing normally?

steps.detail: Lay them on their back and use CPR, adult, CPR, child or CPR, infant. If help has not been called yet, do it now. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Stay with them until help takes over. Keep watching their breathing.
steps.detail: Keep watching breathing and alertness. Keep any remaining auto-injector within reach in case signs continue or return.

steps.text: No epinephrine: sit them up or lie them down as their breathing and condition allow, and watch them closely.
steps.detail:
Without epinephrine, first aid is supportive. Help them into the position they find easiest to breathe in, or lie them down if they show signs of shock. Keep them from getting cold or overheated. Reassure them.

Ask others nearby whether anyone carries an epinephrine auto-injector.

Getting them to medical care is the priority.

ask.q: Have they become unresponsive and stopped breathing normally?

donts: Do not wait for collapse or low blood pressure before giving epinephrine.
Do not leave the person alone.
Do not assume they are safe because they improved; they still need medical care.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently anyone with anaphylaxis, even if they improve after epinephrine.
Evacuate urgently anyone who needed a second dose or who has trouble breathing or signs of shock.
notes: Epinephrine auto-injector: outer middle thigh, straight in until it clicks, hold 3 seconds. Second dose may be given 5 to 10 minutes later if signs continue.
